name: Supercharged skin IV drips

card.summary: Non-medical vitamin, antioxidant and glutathione infusions marketed to give a brighter, clearer, more even skin tone.
card.aka: beauty IV infusions; glow drips; Myers cocktail-style drips
card.note: Regulators in the Philippines and dermatologists have warned about IV glutathione for skin lightening; infusions carry general IV risks.

quick.overview:
Beauty IV drips are infusions of vitamins, minerals and antioxidants such as vitamin C or glutathione, offered at wellness clinics, spas and salons with the aim of a brighter, glowier or lighter complexion. People choose them hoping skin appearance improves from the inside.

They build on the vitamin-IV format popularised by Myers' cocktail and boutique IV clinics. Dermatologists quoted in news coverage report that no published clinical trials show injectable glutathione lightens skin.
quick.how: Clients attend a clinic, spa or salon, where a bag of solution is given through a vein over a session, sometimes as part of a series. Menus are often named for the skin goal, for example glow or brightening, and may be combined with other cosmetic services. Providers describe results appearing over repeated sessions.
quick.risks: Reported risks include those of any IV: pain, infection, vein inflammation and fluid or electrolyte disturbances. For glutathione and high-dose vitamin C specifically, dermatologists have cautioned about effects on liver, kidneys and nerves, kidney stones and reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and the Philippine FDA has said no injectable product is approved for skin lightening. Practitioners advise that infusions be given only under a doctor.

lead: Supercharged skin IV drips are intravenous infusions marketed for skin benefits: brightness, glow, tone and clarity. They typically include vitamins, minerals, antioxidants and, in some offerings, glutathione. They are sold outside conventional medicine, in wellness clinics, spas and salons.

The format descends from the Myers' cocktail, a non-prescription vitamin and mineral IV mix developed by John Myers in the 1960s and marketed for general wellness, and from the boutique IV clinics that began opening in Tokyo in 2008 and gained celebrity customers in the 2010s [1].

Clients use them in the hope that nutrients delivered directly to the bloodstream will improve skin appearance. Medical bodies and dermatologists have commented mainly on skin-lightening drips, warning that no trials show benefit and noting safety concerns [2].

chain: Claimed effect on skin brightness and pigment
angle.text: Clinics promote the drips as a way to deliver nutrients that brighten and even out skin. The effect on appearance is claimed by providers; dermatologists report no trial evidence for glutathione lightening.

infobox: Vitamin C, other vitamins, minerals, glutathione
Philippine FDA: no injectable approved for skin lightening [2]

paras: Wikipedia describes the Myers' cocktail as a non-prescription IV mixture of vitamins and minerals marketed as a hangover cure and general wellness remedy, and notes that the first boutique IV clinic opened in Tokyo in 2008 [1]. Beauty versions apply the same delivery method with skin-focused ingredients, including reduced glutathione and vitamin C offered by salons and clinics [2].
Providers and clients describe the drips as delivering antioxidants and vitamins that brighten and even skin tone. Skin-lightening versions are marketed for reducing pigment [2].

In a January 2025 news report, Philippine dermatologists said there are no published clinical trials showing that injectable glutathione lightens skin, and that the country's FDA has not approved IV glutathione for skin whitening or any injectable product for skin lightening [2]. The Philippine Dermatological Society president said the infusions are medicines and should be given only by a licensed doctor or by a nurse under a doctor's supervision [2].

The report lists possible toxic effects on liver, kidneys and nervous system, concern about Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and kidney stones when glutathione is paired with IV vitamin C in acidic urine [2]. It also notes that large vitamin C doses led to hemodialysis in patients with G6PD deficiency [2].

General IV therapy risks listed by Wikipedia include pain at insertion, infection that can progress to sepsis, phlebitis, infiltration damaging tissue and electrolyte disturbance from unbalanced solutions, with risk higher with improper technique and little oversight [1].
No studies found of non-medical beauty IV drips for skin appearance. Dermatologists quoted in news coverage state that no published trials exist for injectable glutathione skin lightening [2].

timeline.event: John Myers develops the Myers' cocktail [1].
First boutique IV clinic opens in Tokyo [1].
Philippine dermatologists issue warnings about IV glutathione for skin whitening [2].
